What a fundamental misunderstanding of the actual purpose of the Fair Housing Act. The FHA specifically prohibits discrimination on the basis of race to create a system in which people can live wherever they can afford to live. In part, the idea was to end a system in which governments imposed a top-down vision of the "ideal" racial demography of an area; remarkably HUD seems to want to re-institute the same system at a federal level, just with a different "ideal" to impose. Apparently people should be free to choose where to live - unless they want to live in a neighborhood that doesn't fit HUD's vision.

On top of that, this sort of demographic engineering makes even less sense on an economic level. Judging by its statements, HUD seeks to transform all neighborhoods into middle class neighborhoods by moving people of all classes into them; this is a recipe for disaster, and most of all for the people it claims to want to help. If a history of population movements has taught us anything, it's that middle classes moving into low-income neighborhoods drives up housing prices such that working class people can no longer afford to live there and are forced to move out. Normally this evens itself out naturally, but with HUD trying to deliberately disrupt the natural distribution, they'll be playing a perverse game of whack-a-mole, chasing working class people out of their homes again and again, all the while wondering how "class segregation" keeps popping up again.

Gentrification certainly does drive up housing prices and drives those with lower incomes out of city centers. Government interference isn't the answer, and they certainly shouldn't be involved in the housing markets at all. Let the neighborhoods develop organically, let people live where they can afford, and decide who they want to live around. The government shouldn't be forcibly integrating societies or vastly varied socioeconomic classes. For better or worse, we live in a balanced society. Forcing markets never turn out the way you expect, and statistically there is a much higher probability of bad outcomes than positive outcomes.

While we are talking about understanding, can you explain the "disparate impact" method and how it works?

Is it really "demographic engineering"?

Depends on what you mean by "engineering." I would describe it more as a circular argument.

Essentially, the term "disparate impact" is derived from a series of US Supreme Court cases determining what counts as a "discriminatory" statute or rule such that it is unconstitutional. People arguing those cases have proposed that "disparate impact" should be used, meaning that any statute which has differential effects on a minority group is discriminatory. The court has instead held that, at least on a constitutional level, that isn't enough, and one must show a discriminatory intent. To see these two standards in action, consider physical fitness tests for police, which women almost invariably pass less often than men. Under the intent standard, those tests aren't discriminatory unless intended to exclude women, while under the disparate impact analysis, they are discriminatory because women are actually less likely to pass.

What this means from HUD's point of view is a difference in underlying assumption. The disparate impact approach presumes that in the absence of discrimination, everything would be equal; therefore, if anything is unequal, discrimination must exist, and HUD must take action to end it, proving its own assumption by "returning" neighborhoods to class and race diversity. Hence the circularity.

Great response. The Constitutional standard is "discriminatory intent" which is virtually impossible to prove short of a statement almost as bad as "We are making this rule to keep our white area free of blacks."

The disparate impact standard remains intact where a statute uses language that indicates the legislature intended the law to look at the effects. Although some have proposed that such a race consideration is Unconstitutional, courts have held otherwise. The recent FHA decision indicated that the statutory language was effects-oriented, not intent-oriented (5-4 decision of course).

Now to disparate impact -- which is what these articles should have discussed because it is the heart of the matter on this regulation propagation.

First, a regulation or law must be "race neutral."

Then, it must have "effects-based' language.

Once it is determined to be race neutral and effects-based, we have to look at its impact.

If there is no disparate impact of the regulation -- in other words, if the regulation does not increase segregation (in this case) -- then, the regulation is good. End of story.

If there is a disparate impact of the regulation, then we move to the next step.

We ask now, given that this regulation increases segregation, can we find a less discriminatory regulation to achieve the same goals?

If we can, then we must shift to it. If we cannot, then we can keep it the way it is.

While perusing through some new subverses ( /v/90smusic to be exact ) I noticed a bug with the pagination when sorting by "Top" submissions.

If you go into a subverse and sort by "Top" it defaults to the "day" timeframe and pagination works fine. The problem arises when you select any timeframe other than "day". A new argument is added to the URL and you get /top?time=week - but when you attempt to hit "next" in the pagination, the link takes you to /top?page=1 which omits the time= argument and thus reverts you back to "day" view.

This mechanism works the same for any of the timeframes, except for the default "day", because there is no argument added to the URL with that option.

The code DOES work, if you manually add to the URL &page=1 - increasing the page number to cycle through the older pages e.g: /top?time=week&page=1

I imagine it's just a simple fix adding the time= argument to the "next" and "previous" buttons at the bottom of each page, but I haven't taken a look at the code to be sure. Hope this makes sense to everyone!

EDIT: It seems this has already been pointed out by @yuvallevental here and on github as well - Sorry about that!
